title: Evaluate extension services in a simple setting

lessons.title: Why and what we evaluate in extension
lessons.html:
The purpose of evaluation

Evaluation is the systematic assessment of whether an extension service is doing what it set out to do, how well, and why. Departments of agriculture, donors and commodity organisations invest public and private money in extension, and they need evidence that it makes a difference. Evaluation also helps the practitioner learn and improve.

Monitoring versus evaluation

MonitoringEvaluation
Ongoing tracking of activities and outputsPeriodic assessment of results and impact
Example: number of farm visits per monthExample: did maize yields of participating farmers improve?
Done mainly by the practitionerMay involve independent evaluators and farmers

The results chain

  1. Inputs - staff time, vehicle, budget, materials.
  2. Activities - demonstrations, training, farm visits.
  3. Outputs - number of farmers trained, demonstrations held.
  4. Outcomes - changes in knowledge, practice and production, such as farmers keeping herd records.
  5. Impact - longer-term changes such as higher household income or improved food security.

Many reports stop at outputs: 120 farmers attended an information day. This tells us little. Good evaluation asks what changed for those farmers. However, impact is influenced by many factors outside extension, such as rainfall and prices, so be careful when claiming that a change was caused by your service.

Common evaluation criteria

  • Relevance - does the service address the farmers' real needs?
  • Effectiveness - were the objectives achieved?
  • Efficiency - were resources used well?
  • Impact - what longer-term changes occurred?
  • Sustainability - will benefits continue after support ends?

lessons.title: Planning an evaluation and collecting data
lessons.html:
Designing a simple evaluation

Consider a programme in which a practitioner supported 30 smallholder goat farmers in KwaZulu-Natal over a year with training on parasite control and kid management. A simple evaluation can be planned in a few steps.

Planning steps

  1. Define the purpose and users. Who will use the findings: the farmers, your manager, a funder?
  2. Write evaluation questions. For example: Did kid survival improve? Which practices were adopted? What did farmers find most and least useful?
  3. Choose indicators. Kid survival rate, number of farmers keeping treatment records, farmers' satisfaction rating.
  4. Find baseline information. What was the situation before the programme? Without a baseline it is hard to show change.
  5. Select methods and sample. Decide whether to include all 30 farmers or a sample, and whether to compare with non-participating farmers.
  6. Plan logistics and ethics. Time, transport, translators and informed consent.

Data collection methods

  • Records - attendance registers, farm records, visit reports.
  • Questionnaires - structured questions, useful for numbers.
  • Interviews - with individual farmers or key informants such as the local animal health technician.
  • Focus group discussions - 6 to 10 people discussing their experience.
  • Observation - walking the farm to see whether a practice is really in place.
  • Participatory tools - scoring, before-and-after drawings, most significant change stories.

Combine numbers (quantitative data) with stories and explanations (qualitative data). Numbers show what changed; stories explain why.

Ethics

Explain the purpose, ask permission, protect personal information and do not promise benefits for taking part.

lessons.title: Analysing, reporting and using findings
lessons.html:
From data to improvement

Data is only useful if it is analysed honestly and used to improve the service.

Simple analysis

  • Count and calculate percentages, for example the share of farmers now deworming based on need rather than on a fixed calendar.
  • Compare before and after, and participants with non-participants where possible.
  • Group interview answers into themes, such as cost of medicines, distance to the co-op or poor transport.
  • Look for unexpected results, both positive and negative.
  • Check whether outside factors, like drought or a disease outbreak, may explain the results.

Writing the evaluation report

  1. Summary of key findings and recommendations on the first page.
  2. Background and objectives of the service.
  3. Methods used and their limitations.
  4. Findings organised by evaluation question.
  5. Conclusions and practical recommendations.

Keep language plain and use small tables. Be honest about what did not work; hiding failures prevents learning.

Feeding back to farmers

Share results with the farmers who provided the information, in a meeting and in their language. Ask whether the findings make sense to them. This builds trust and often adds new insights.

Using findings

Agree on actions: for example, change the timing of training to fit the farming calendar, add a mentor visit, or link farmers to a supplier of medicines closer to home. Record the decisions and check later whether they were implemented.

Key points

  • Monitoring tracks activities; evaluation assesses results and impact.
  • Use the results chain from inputs to impact, and do not stop at outputs.
  • Plan evaluation questions, indicators, baseline and methods before collecting data.
  • Combine numbers with farmers' stories and explanations.
  • Report honestly, feed back to farmers and act on findings.
